extracted.intended_audience: photojournalists, journalism students, editors, and readers interested in media ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Discussion of ethical standards and practical guidelines governing digital photo manipulation in journalism, advertising, fashion, academia, and other media contexts. Explains what alterations are commonly permitted, forbidden, and how institutions enforce standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: No substantial digital manipulation in news media
rubrics_metrics.description: Major news purveyors — print, broadcast and online — have strict policies against digital manipulation of photographs, and substantial manipulation is regarded as unacceptable in responsible news media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states that such manipulation is rare in responsible outlets and that violators face severe penalties (summary termination). Examples: The New York Times published a correction after an employee altered a photo (April 2007); the L.A. Times photographer was fired for digitally removing trees from an Iraq shot. Emphasizes expectation of visual truth in news photography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted minor alterations for contrast and clarity (must not change the story)
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor changes that improve visibility or clarity are allowed only when they 'did not change the story' or meaning of the picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible techniques cited include enhancing a foreground figure, creating more contrast between foreground and background, cropping, and lighting changes 'if these alterations did not change the meaning of the picture.' Historical analogues: dodging and burning from darkroom practice are considered similar in intent to some digital adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbidden: adding or removing people or objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers must not insert or remove people or objects in images, since such actions change the factual content and meaning of a photo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct quotes include 'You couldn't put people in a shot or take anyone out' and 'you can't remove an object. And you can't change the meaning of a photograph.' Example: Two government officials were digitally removed from a White House photograph (Di Tzeitung incident). Such changes are grounds for dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulated images are illustrations, not news photographs
rubrics_metrics.description: If a photograph is digitally manipulated in ways that alter its factual content or presentation, it should be treated as an illustration rather than a news photograph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold Crane: 'A digitally manipulated photograph is an illustration, not a news photograph.' This classification affects whether the image is appropriate for news contexts and whether it requires labeling or different use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising and fashion routinely alter images but must not misrepresent products
rubrics_metrics.description: Altering images to flatter subjects or improve aesthetics is common in advertising and fashion, but alterations that misrepresent product features are unethical and sometimes regulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices such as making people look thinner or younger, smoothing complexions, or enhancing food appearance are widespread ('practically every photo for advertising purposes has been altered'). However, 'faking product features' (example: a brownie showing more nuts than actually present) is unacceptable; the advertising industry and government regulations forbid misrepresentation in ads and commercials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable minor retouching in portraits (subject to debate and newsroom policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some minor retouching (e.g., removing blemishes) can be acceptable in portraits, but acceptance varies by practitioner and organizational policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold Crane described removing a zit from a portrait as acceptable and analogous to darkroom retouching. Other outlets may be stricter. The boundary between innocuous retouching and unethical alteration is contested and often governed by newsroom rules or codes (e.g., NPPA standards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional/academic materials should not be manipulated to misrepresent facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Altering photographs or promotional materials to misrepresent institutional demographics, achievements or realities is unethical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: University of Wisconsin brochure altered to include a black male in a crowd to 'proclaim the diversity' of the student body — cited as an instance of unethical manipulation in academia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement: corrections, watchdogs, and disciplinary action
rubrics_metrics.description: When manipulation is discovered, news organizations publish corrections and impose sanctions; both in-house and external watchdogs monitor for photo fakery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New York Times issued a correction for an altered image; the article notes that there are in-house and outside vigilantes 'ever vigilant for photo fakery' ready to blow the whistle and committed to punishing violators, including firing and refusal to buy a photographer's work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freelancer responsibilities and market consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Freelance photojournalists are self-employed and thus governed primarily by their own integrity, but manipulation harms marketability and can result in editors refusing future purchases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece notes freelancers may enhance photos to sell them, but if caught substantially manipulating images, 'media editors aware of the deception would probably never again buy the freelancer’s work.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/political manipulation common under authoritarian regimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Official photographs issued by dictatorial or totalitarian regimes may be doctored for propaganda, making such images untrustworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In the former Soviet Union Josef Stalin had dissidents removed from official photos using airbrushing; modern digital tools make such manipulations far easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for formal education and training in photojournalistic ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethics training for photojournalists has moved from on-the-job verbal instruction to formal coursework in many colleges and journalism programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recounts that earlier photographers were trained verbally by editors and learned on the job, but 'many colleges and universities offer courses in the ethics and legalities of photojournalism' today.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish context: editorial vs. illustrative vs. advertising usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards differ by context: rigorous truthfulness is required in news/editorial uses, while advertising/fashion might permissibly alter images for aesthetics — though not to deceive about products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article repeatedly underscores different expectations across contexts: mainstream media disallow manipulations that change meaning; advertising/fashion routinely retouch for appearance; publicity photographs of celebrities are routinely altered to flatter subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to professional codes (e.g., NPPA standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers should follow codified ethical standards (the National Press Photographers Association is cited) that define acceptable and unacceptable photo practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold Crane states he 'subscribes entirely to the ethical standards of The National Press Photographers Association.' The piece implies that adherence to such codes informs newsroom policy and personal practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and correction when manipulation is discovered
rubrics_metrics.description: When manipulation happens in journalistic contexts, organizations should correct the record and be transparent about the error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New York Times example: published a correction and noted its policy against photographic alteration. Watchdog role and corrections are part of restoring trust after manipulation is revealed.
